title: RAG Optimization and Evaluation
why: Lecture 11's RAG sometimes finds the wrong part — especially on exact words (“B-2”, “12%”). But “sometimes” isn't a number, and “I think it's better” doesn't count. In real teams every RAG change — chunking, the search method, the prompt — is proven by measurement. Today we measure (golden set, hit@k, MRR), improve (hybrid search, filtering, chunking) and check the answer's groundedness.
outcomes: You'll explain where RAG fails (retrieval vs generation), put together a golden set and calculate hit@3 and MRR with `/rag/eval`
You'll build hybrid search: the vector + PostgreSQL full-text (`tsvector`, `'english'`), merged with RRF, and prove the improvement with a number
You'll add metadata filtering in SQL and explain why it's also a security matter
You'll compare chunking strategies and reranking, and evaluate the answer's groundedness with `GroundednessEvaluator`

review.q: In which two places does RAG fail, and which one is more common?
review.a: retrieval — the right part didn't get into the top k (the most common; then even the best model can't answer) · generation — the part is right, but the model added something that isn't in the source

review.q: What are hit@3 and MRR? Why do we write a phrase in the golden set and not the chunk's Id?
review.a: hit@3 — on what share of the questions the right part was in the top three · MRR — the average 1/rank, how high it is · when the chunking changes the Ids change, the phrase doesn't

review.q: Why do we need hybrid search, and why do we merge the lists by rank (RRF) and not by scores?
review.a: the vector finds exact words (a code, a number, a name) badly, full-text finds them exactly · the scores are in different “units”, the rank is the same everywhere: Σ 1/(60 + rank)

review.q: Why must metadata filtering be in SQL and not in the prompt?
review.a: the model doesn't always obey the prompt; if someone else's part got into the context, it has already leaked · a tenant/permissions filter is security, before the model

review.q: What is groundedness and how do we measure it? Why don't we trust the judge completely?
review.a: does the answer rely only on the sources? · LLM-as-judge: GroundednessEvaluator, 1–5 and an explanation · the judge is a model too — it makes mistakes and rates its own answers softly; on many examples and manually from time to time

quiz.q: We changed the chunk size from 800 to 400. It got better on two questions. The right conclusion:
options: We can't say anything yet — we have to measure on the golden set: a change improves some and breaks others
quiz.explain: First we measure, then we change, then we measure again.

options: retrieval — the right part didn't get into the top k, and the model has nothing to answer with
quiz.explain: That's why we measure the search first.

quiz.q: Why do we write a “must appear in the part” phrase in the golden set and not the chunk's Id?
options: When the chunking changes, the parts are cut again and the Ids change — a phrase works with any strategy
EF Core can't read the Id
quiz.explain: A golden set must survive changes.

quiz.q: The `/rag/eval` misses show “Where is hall B-2?” and “12%”. What do they have in common?
options: Exact words — a code and a number that the vector “sees” badly

quiz.q: In `to_tsvector('english', 'Hall B-2 seats 20+ guests')`, what does "guests" become, and why?
options: "guest" — the 'english' configuration has a stemmer; the query must be processed with the same configuration
It's removed — it's a stop word
quiz.explain: Georgian text has no dictionary — there it's 'simple'.

quiz.q: Why does RRF merge two lists by rank?
options: The vector score and ts_rank are in different “units” — adding them makes no sense; the rank is the same everywhere
quiz.explain: Σ 1/(60 + rank): the one high in both lists comes first.

quiz.q: In a multi-client system, where should another client's document be hidden?
options: In the system prompt: “don't show others' documents”
In SQL, before the search — a filter by TenantId; nothing should reach the model
quiz.explain: Getting into the context is already a leak.

quiz.q: Why do we run a reranker only on 20 candidates and not on every part?
options: A cross-encoder reads the question and the part together — it's precise, but nothing can be calculated in advance; on every part it's very slow and expensive. The fast search picks, the reranker sorts
